skill.name: semantic-scholar-library-feed
skill.description: Work with an authenticated Semantic Scholar account to inspect Research Feeds, export private Library folders, resolve paper identifiers, and add papers to folders.
skill.summary: Inspect Semantic Scholar feeds and library folders with authenticated CLI helpers.
skill.author: zjsxply

security_audit.summary: Most command-execution and reconnaissance alerts are false positives from Markdown backticks, help strings, or documented endpoint notes. The real risks are handling reusable Semantic Scholar session cookies, writing private data to local files, outbound authenticated requests, and an unvalidated page URL that can leak cookies. No prompt-injection text was found in the reviewed skill files.

remediation.issue: Unvalidated page URLs receive Cookie headers.
remediation.suggestion: Reject non-Semantic Scholar origins before calling fetch_html, and never attach stored cookies to arbitrary user-supplied URLs.

remediation.issue: Session cookies are stored as plaintext files.
remediation.suggestion: Store cookies with owner-only permissions, avoid writing a raw header file by default, and document secure cleanup steps.

remediation.issue: Folder updates can mutate the user's private library.
remediation.suggestion: Make dry-run the default for folder-add and require explicit user confirmation before authenticated POST requests.

remediation.issue: Examples use /tmp for sensitive curl input and private exports.
remediation.suggestion: Use a private working directory for copied curl files, cookies, feed exports, and folder exports.

semantic_findings.title: Unvalidated URL Can Receive Session Cookies
semantic_findings.description: The CLI accepts a page URL for SSR and feed bootstrapping, then fetches it with the stored Cookie header. A malicious or mistaken URL can receive reusable Semantic Scholar session cookies.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The code attaches Cookie headers whenever a bundle is present, while ssr-dump and feed-crawl accept page URLs without origin validation. This is a direct credential disclosure path.

semantic_findings.title: Plaintext Semantic Scholar Session Cookie Storage
semantic_findings.description: The workflow imports browser session cookies and writes both structured cookies and a raw Cookie header to local files. These files can be reused to access private Library and Research Feed data.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The documentation explicitly requires sid and s2 cookies, and the implementation writes the raw header to disk. The behavior is intentional but exposes high-value account credentials if file access is weak.

semantic_findings.title: Authenticated Library Mutation Without Built-In Confirmation
semantic_findings.description: The skill includes a folder-add command that posts to Semantic Scholar's bulk library endpoint. Without a required confirmation step, an agent can modify the user's private library once cookies are available.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The documented workflow and implementation perform an authenticated POST that changes folder membership. A dry-run flag exists, but confirmation is not enforced by the command.

content.value_statement: Researchers need repeatable access to Semantic Scholar feeds and private library folders. This skill provides CLI workflows for authenticated feed export, folder inspection, and paper resolution.
actual_capabilities: Imports Semantic Scholar cookies from a copied browser curl command or raw Cookie header.
Checks whether required session cookies are present before private requests run.
Decodes Semantic Scholar recommendation page SSR data for feed bootstrapping.
Crawls Research Feed recommendation windows and saves progress incrementally.
Exports private Library folder entries with pagination and filters.
Resolves arXiv, DOI, or Corpus identifiers through Semantic Scholar Graph batch lookups.
limitations: It requires user-provided authenticated Semantic Scholar cookies for private account data.
It stores session cookies locally unless the workflow is changed by the user.
Semantic Scholar private endpoints are unofficial and may change without notice.
Folder add operations can modify the user's Semantic Scholar library.

use_cases.title: Export a Research Feed
use_cases.description: Collect recommendation windows for later review, filtering, or archiving.

use_cases.title: Audit a Library Folder
use_cases.description: List folder entries, compare them with a bibliography, and identify missing papers.

use_cases.title: Resolve Paper Identifiers
use_cases.description: Convert arXiv or DOI identifiers into Semantic Scholar paper records before folder updates.

prompt_templates.title: Check Cookie Readiness
prompt_templates.prompt: Check whether my Semantic Scholar cookie store is ready. Tell me which cookies are missing and what I should refresh.

prompt_templates.title: Export Feed History
prompt_templates.prompt: Crawl my Semantic Scholar Research Feed and save each window as progress is made. Stop when pagination is complete.

prompt_templates.title: Compare Folder to Bibliography
prompt_templates.prompt: Export my target Semantic Scholar folder, resolve identifiers from my bibliography, and report which papers are missing.

prompt_templates.title: Prepare Safe Folder Updates
prompt_templates.prompt: Resolve these paper identifiers, show the proposed folder additions first, and only add papers after I approve the final list.

output_examples.input: Check whether my cookie store is usable.
output: Reports whether the cookie file exists.
Lists missing required cookie names without printing full cookie values.
Recommends importing a fresh browser curl when required cookies are absent.

output_examples.input: Export my feed for local screening.
output: Creates a saved feed crawl with window counts and paper counts.
Records the stop reason, such as no next window or duplicate window.
Preserves recommendation metadata for later local review.

output_examples.input: Resolve these arXiv identifiers before adding them to a folder.
output: Returns matching Semantic Scholar paper records for the supplied identifiers.
Deduplicates repeated identifiers before the batch lookup.
Can save the resolved records for review before any folder update.

best_practices: Use a private, user-controlled directory for cookies and exported private data.
Review proposed folder additions before running any command that changes the library.
Refresh cookies from a successful Semantic Scholar browser request when private endpoints return 401.
anti_patterns: Do not paste authenticated curl commands into shared terminals or logs.
Do not store Semantic Scholar session cookies in shared temporary directories.
Do not run folder-add until the target folder and paper list are confirmed.

faq.question: Does this skill need my Semantic Scholar password?
faq.answer: No. It uses cookies copied from an already authenticated browser session.

faq.question: Can it read private Library folders?
faq.answer: Yes, when valid session cookies are available and the account has access to those folders.

faq.question: Can it change my Semantic Scholar account?
faq.answer: Yes. The folder-add workflow can add papers to Library folders.

faq.question: Does it use official Semantic Scholar APIs only?
faq.answer: No. It uses the public Graph API and private web endpoints observed from Semantic Scholar pages.

faq.question: Will it hide my cookie values in every output?
faq.answer: The cookie summary masks cookie headers, but imported curl files and cookie stores remain sensitive.

faq.question: Can Claude, Codex, and Claude Code use this skill?
faq.answer: Yes. The report lists support for Claude, Codex, and Claude Code.
